simulatedReaderProbe.prompt: Why might an AI trained on usual preserved tissue slides need separate frozen-image training during surgery?
simulatedReaderProbe.probeResponse: Frozen tissue has a different appearance, so a model trained on usual preserved slides may not have learned the patterns it needs. CRISP was trained for frozen images, while a pathologist still interprets its prediction.
simulatedReaderProbe.expectedEvidence: Distinguish the image-preparation difference from the model-comparison result.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: Most existing foundation models are built upon FFPE specimens, which differ fundamentally from frozen sections in both preparation and tissue morphology. Direct application of FFPE-trained models to intraoperative frozen section risks compromising diagnostic accuracy as such models may lack exposure to frozen section morphology.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: In an observational study — researchers watched normal care — it beat other AI models. A reader study, comparing answers with specialists, found it matched the senior specialist overall.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: Crucially, CRISP demonstrated consistent superiority over competing foundation models across independent prospective external cohorts. In a reader study conducted on the prospective SYCC cohort, the operating point of the senior pathologist fell on the ROC curve of CRISP, indicating comparable overall performance under the evaluated conditions.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: A simulated deployment analysis ran CRISP through 100 cases in a row to estimate timing; it did not change live care. The authors still need a study that changes care and follows patients.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: In a simulated deployment experiment conducted on 100 cases from SYCC, the average end-to-end processing time for CRISP was 196.4 seconds per case, compared to 292.6 seconds for pathologists.
a fully prospective interventional study is still necessary to assess its real-world deployment and impact on clinical outcomes.
